articles.title: Millions Turn to Turmeric for Joint Pain. Does It Really Work?
articles.dek: A closer examination of clinical trial reliability raises new questions about earlier research suggesting turmeric could help people with knee osteoarthritis.
paragraphs: A closer examination of clinical trial reliability raises new questions about earlier research suggesting turmeric could help people with knee osteoarthritis.

Turmeric supplements are widely promoted as a natural way to ease joint pain, but a major new scientific review has cast doubt on their effectiveness for knee osteoarthritis. Researchers found little convincing evidence that the popular supplements provide clinically meaningful pain relief, challenging earlier studies that suggested they could help.

The findings come from a new Cochrane review that examined both the results of clinical trials and the reliability of the research behind them. Although the evidence remains uncertain, the analysis found no clear advantage for turmeric over placebo or commonly used anti-inflammatory medications.

The international research team analyzed nine studies involving 1,245 people with knee osteoarthritis. The trials compared turmeric supplements with placebo, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and diclofenac, and paracetamol. Participants received different turmeric extracts and curcuminoid formulations, with treatment periods ranging from four weeks to three months.

Turmeric contains curcuminoids, including curcumin, which have anti-inflammatory properties. These compounds have attracted interest as potential treatments for osteoarthritis, a disease involving damage and changes throughout the joint. Inflammation can contribute to pain and other symptoms, but the condition has multiple underlying causes. Exercise and medications can help manage symptoms, although no cure currently exists.

Previous systematic reviews generally reported improvements in pain and physical function among people taking turmeric supplements. However, the new Cochrane analysis applied more rigorous screening procedures to assess whether individual clinical trials were trustworthy enough to support reliable conclusions.

Ten trials raised concerns during this screening process and were excluded from the analysis while researchers sought clarification from their authors. Earlier reviews had also included broader categories of studies, such as those involving osteoarthritis diagnosed solely through imaging, non-oral turmeric treatments, or curcumin combined with other active ingredients. These methodological differences may partly explain the conflicting conclusions.

“This review highlights the importance of assessing the trustworthiness of clinical trials,” adds Dr Shirinsky. “Such assessments help identify studies that require further clarification before their findings can be used to inform conclusions about treatment effects.”

The researchers used a screening method developed by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth group. Other approaches, including INSPECT-SR , have since been developed to identify potentially problematic studies before their findings influence scientific reviews.
Dr. Ivan Shirinsky, the review’s lead author and a practicing rheumatologist, said the results reflect the broader challenges of treating a disease with complex biological mechanisms.

“As a clinician and researcher, I am not surprised by these findings. Osteoarthritis is a complex and still incompletely understood disease. Despite intensive research, effective pharmacological treatment options remain limited, and many promising approaches have yielded limited or inconclusive evidence of clinical benefit. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying osteoarthritis may help us develop more effective treatments in the future.”

The review does not establish that turmeric supplements are ineffective in every circumstance. Rather, the available research does not provide sufficiently reliable evidence of a clinically important benefit. Shirinsky said this uncertainty would shape how he advises patients considering turmeric for knee pain.

“I would not routinely recommend turmeric supplements to my patients with knee osteoarthritis. However, if a patient asked me about them, I would explain what we know and what remains uncertain about their benefits and potential harms, and help them make an informed decision.”

articles.title: Taking Weight-Loss Drugs? New Study Reveals Why Lifting Weights Could Be Essential
articles.dek: As weight-loss medications become increasingly common, a clinical trial suggests that three weekly strength-training sessions could help people preserve muscle and maintain…
paragraphs: As weight-loss medications become increasingly common, a clinical trial suggests that three weekly strength-training sessions could help people preserve muscle and maintain physical independence.
Losing weight is often the goal for people taking medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, but the number on the scale does not tell the whole story.

A new study found that adults taking a powerful weight-loss drug shed nearly 50 pounds in 40 weeks, regardless of whether they exercised. Those who also lifted weights, however, preserved more lean tissue and became stronger, while participants who did not train experienced a decline in strength.

The findings address a growing concern surrounding medications such as semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro). These drugs can produce substantial weight loss and have been found to improve chronic health conditions, reduce the risk of obesity-related cardiovascular disease, and enhance quality of life. However, losing so much weight raises questions about how much muscle people might lose along the way.

“Loss of lean mass, including muscle, is an inevitable part of weight loss by any method – whether through diet and exercise alone, or medical or surgical interventions,” said Winthrop Professor Danny Green, lead investigator from The University of Western Australia’s School of Human Sciences and HealthSpan Institute.

Lean mass includes everything in the body other than fat, such as muscles, bones, organs, skin, and water. Muscle mass refers specifically to muscle tissue, mostly skeletal muscle. Preserving that tissue is particularly important for people hoping to maintain their strength and physical independence as they lose weight.

“With GLP-1 medicines now widely used and reducing body weight by an average of 20-25 percent, and more than that in many people, it’s crucial that we understand how best to achieve optimal body composition and health in the weight-reduced state.”

To investigate whether exercise could help, researchers conducted the Tirzepatide and Resistance Exercise (T-REx) study, published in Nature Medicine . It is the first study to examine the combined effects of a GLP-1 medication and resistance training on body composition, muscle mass, strength, and a range of cardiovascular health measures.

The 40-week trial involved 120 men and postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 70. All participants had obesity or were overweight with at least one weight-related health condition. None had type 2 diabetes, and all were prescribed tirzepatide for weight management.

Half the participants completed three resistance-training sessions each week, while the others did not follow a resistance-training program. Everyone received general guidance on hydration, protein consumption, and fiber intake.

By the end of the study, both groups had experienced substantial weight loss. Participants who exercised lost an average of 22. 28 kilograms (49. 1 pounds), compared with 22. 61 kilograms (49. 8 pounds) among those who did not train.

Most of that weight loss came from fat. The resistance-training group lost an average of 17. 98 kilograms (39. 6 pounds) of fat mass, while the group without resistance training lost 17. 19 kilograms (37. 9 pounds).

The more meaningful difference emerged when researchers examined lean tissue and physical strength. Participants who lifted weights lost 25 percent less lean tissue, including muscle, than those who did not exercise. Their upper- and lower-body strength also increased by 10 percent, compared with a 10 percent decline among participants who did not undertake resistance training.
“We now know that muscle loss can be reduced and strength increased when regular resistance training is used alongside tirzepatide treatment.”

articles.title: Silver briefly forms a rare crystal structure seen in radioactive polonium
articles.dek: How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties.
paragraphs: How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties. The same carbon atoms, for example, can form diamond and graphite depending on how they are arranged, giving rise to materials with vastly different chemical and physical properties. Now, researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a new crystal structure of silver with unusually high chemical reactivity. The findings, published in Nano Letters , could open new avenues for exploring materials with desirable properties.

Silver normally forms a repeating cube-shaped structure, with atoms located at each of the cube's eight corners and at the center of each face. This arrangement is known as a face-centered cubic crystal structure and is common among metals, including aluminum, copper and gold. In the new study, researchers observed that under certain conditions, silver atoms can adopt a simple cubic structure, in which the atoms occupy only the eight corners of a cube that repeats in three dimensions.
Simple cubic structures are exceptionally rare among elements. One other example is the radioactive element polonium.

In this study, researchers used an electron beam to trigger the decomposition of silver iodide, observing the newly formed silver atoms arrange themselves into a previously unreported simple cubic structure.

At the nanoscale, where materials measure just a few billionths of a meter, structures that are unstable in larger materials can sometimes emerge temporarily. Studying these structures gives researchers an opportunity to discover materials with unique properties that are not found in their conventional forms.

Under high-vacuum conditions, the new simple cubic silver behaved differently from ordinary silver. While conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, simple cubic silver gradually oxidized to form silver oxide. This indicated unusually high chemical reactivity in the new structure.

"It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal," says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. "We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn't expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure."

The team used a transmission electron microscope (TEM) both to trigger the chemical transformation of silver iodide and to observe the process at the atomic scale. A TEM uses a beam of electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light, allowing it to reveal individual atoms. By combining the ability to induce chemical change with real-time atomic-scale imaging, the researchers could directly observe how the new silver crystal structure emerged. "Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide," adds Sakakibara.

"This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future," says professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University. "Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds."

articles.title: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson
articles.dek: For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed…
paragraphs: For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk.

Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.” Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science ( ARES ) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one. In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations.

articles.title: Atmospheric organic nitrogen emerges as a major nutrient source for global oceans
articles.dek: A research team has quantified an important component of the global nitrogen cycle.
paragraphs: A research team has quantified an important component of the global nitrogen cycle.

The study reveals that 12. 8 million tonnes of organic nitrogen (ON) are deposited from the atmosphere into the global oceans annually, constituting approximately 27% of total nitrogen deposition. In nitrogen-limited waters such as the central Atlantic Ocean and the Indonesian seas, ON contributes around half of total nitrogen deposition. These new findings reshape the understanding of marine nutrient supply and its impacts on ocean ecosystems and climate.

The paper, titled " Atmospheric Organic Nitrogen is a Major Nutrient Source to Global Oceans ," is published in the journal Science . The researchers were co-led by Yu Jianzhen, chair professor in the Department of Chemistry and the Division of Environment and Sustainability at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), and Fu Tzung-May, professor in the School of Environmental Science and Engineering at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech).
Airborne nitrogen deposited into the oceans supports marine life, yet the contribution of ON to this flux has remained unclear due to its chemical complexity and long-standing measurement challenges.

To address this knowledge gap, the research team, in collaboration with researchers from Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, East China Normal University, Ocean University of China, South China University of Technology and HKUST (Guangzhou), combined an innovative atmospheric ON measurement method with extensive open-ocean and polar marine observations and a global atmospheric chemistry model to quantify ON deposition.

Yu stated, "Our study demonstrates that atmospheric ON is far from a minor player in marine ecosystems. Rather, it is a vital nutrient source for global oceans that has often been overlooked. Through an innovative measurement method, coupled with cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers in atmospheric observations, atmospheric modeling, marine science and polar research, we were able to quantify this crucial biogeochemical link between the atmosphere and marine ecosystems."

Traditional methods measure ON by subtracting inorganic nitrogen (IN) from total nitrogen—an error-prone and laborious approach that has left major gaps in global data sets. To address these gaps, the team previously developed a high-sensitivity analytical method capable of simultaneously measuring both aerosol ON and IN.

In the present study, the team applied this method to 418 marine aerosol samples from 21 research cruises, including multiple expeditions to the Arctic and Antarctic. The samples spanned a wide range of oceanic regions, from the tropical to the polar oceans, including the Arctic and Southern oceans, producing the most comprehensive ON data set to date.

The results revealed that aerosol ON concentrations varied by over three orders of magnitude, ranging from below 0. 01 μg N m⁻³ over the remote Southern Ocean to above 10 μg N m⁻³ over the Yellow Sea along the western margin of the Pacific Ocean. On average, ON accounted for 30% of total aerosol nitrogen.

The team used these extensive measurements to constrain a three-dimensional atmospheric chemistry model of ON, quantifying ON deposition into the global oceans at 12. 8 million tonnes per year. The analysis identified the three largest sources of ON to the oceans as biomass-burning emissions (4. 8 million tonnes annually), marine aerosol emissions (3. 9 million tonnes annually) and imines produced chemically in the atmosphere (2. 2 million tonnes annually). Together, nonmarine sources, such as wildfires and human activities, contribute 8. 9 million tonnes of ON annually, representing 70% of total ON deposited into the oceans.
Fu explained, "These terrestrial sources act as an important external nutrient input that can stimulate open-ocean productivity, and changes in these emissions may affect marine nutrient dynamics."

articles.title: One in Four Consumers Would Pay $225 More for Salmon-Safe Tires. Would You?
articles.dek: In a West Coast survey, one in four consumers said they would pay $225 extra for salmon-safe tires, bringing wildlife conservation into an everyday buying decision.
paragraphs: In a West Coast survey, one in four consumers said they would pay $225 extra for salmon-safe tires, bringing wildlife conservation into an everyday buying decision.

Buying new tires could someday give drivers a way to help protect salmon. A new study suggests that many consumers would pay extra for tires labeled “salmon safe,” potentially creating a market for products designed to reduce harm to fish.

The idea comes from a troubling discovery made several years ago. Research co-led by Washington State University (WSU) scientists found that 6PPD, a chemical added to tires to prevent them from breaking down too quickly, is toxic to coho salmon. When tire debris from roads reaches freshwater streams, the chemical can kill the fish.

Tire manufacturers are now exploring new formulations that would eliminate 6PPD. As that work continues, economists at WSU wanted to understand whether consumers would voluntarily spend more on tires that could help protect salmon.

“The tire doesn’t exist yet, but we wanted to know how the general population might value the tire after it’s been developed,” said Joe Cook, a professor in WSU’s School of Economic Sciences and lead author of the study. “As the tire industry explores reformulation, we hope this demonstrates there is a potential market for ‘eco-labeled’ tires.”

Cook, who works at WSU’s Puyallup Research and Extension Center, conducted the research with Wisnu Sugiarto, a professor at Whitman College and former WSU graduate student. Their findings were published in the journal Marine Resource Economics .

The researchers surveyed nearly 700 residents of California, Oregon, and Washington, asking how much they would be willing to pay for hypothetical salmon-safe tires. They then compared those amounts with what participants reported spending on their most recent tire purchases.

The median willingness to pay was 10% above the previous purchase price, equivalent to roughly $76 more for a set of four tires. That means half of respondents were willing to pay a larger premium, while the other half would pay less.
Some participants placed an even higher value on protecting salmon.

“Approximately 25% of people said they would pay a premium of $225 for a set of four salmon-safe tires,” Cook said. “This shows that protecting salmon is very important for a sizeable group of consumers in the three states.”

The results suggest that environmental concerns could influence an ordinary purchasing decision, even when consumers would have to spend more. For tire manufacturers considering alternatives to 6PPD, that willingness to pay could point to a potential market for products advertised as safer for salmon.

However, the researchers emphasized that what consumers say they would voluntarily pay for an environmentally friendly product is different from what manufacturers might charge if regulations required them to remove 6PPD.

“This study is about voluntary eco-labeling for a hypothetical product,” Cook said. “We aren’t saying that prices would go up this amount if 6PPD is regulated out of tires — that ultimately would depend on what it costs for tire manufacturers to reformulate and how competitive the tire industry is.

“Our results couldn’t be used in a benefit-cost analysis of a state or federal regulation,” he continued. “That would require a different survey approach, but we would be excited to look at that and well-placed to do that work.”

articles.title: Earth’s Ozone Hole Swells to More Than Twice the Size of the United States
articles.dek: An unusually powerful polar vortex caused the Antarctic ozone hole to swell to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, covering more than twice the area of the United States.
paragraphs: An unusually powerful polar vortex caused the Antarctic ozone hole to swell to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, covering more than twice the area of the United States.

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, making it one of the largest observed in nearly five decades. Despite its extraordinary size, scientists from NASA and NOAA emphasize that Earth’s protective ozone layer continues to recover and remains on course to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a powerful circulation of winds surrounding Antarctica. However, they also noted that decades of international efforts to reduce ozone-destroying chemicals prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was most intense, the hole covered an average of approximately 9. 6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone high in the atmosphere because it serves as Earth’s natural “sunscreen,” protecting living organisms from harmful ultraviolet radiation. This beneficial ozone in the stratosphere differs from ground level ozone, an air pollutant often produced by human activities.

“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”

The ozone hole reached its maximum size on September 18, expanding to 10. 5 million square miles (27. 1 million square kilometers). That was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3. 5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said.

Ozone destruction begins with human-made chemicals containing chlorine and bromine. After entering the environment, these compounds gradually rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet sunlight breaks them apart and releases chlorine and bromine atoms. These atoms can then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in clouds that form in the extremely cold Antarctic stratosphere, leading to the breakdown of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the polar vortex, a seasonal ring of strong winds that circulates around Antarctica high in the atmosphere. By trapping exceptionally cold air over the continent, the vortex creates conditions that allow polar stratospheric clouds to develop. These clouds provide an important environment for the chemical reactions responsible for ozone depletion.
In 2026, the polar vortex was unusually extensive because atmospheric disturbances that normally weaken and disrupt it were less active than usual.

“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.”

Although the 2026 ozone hole covered an exceptionally large area, the amount of ozone lost within it was less severe than during some of the most extreme depletion events recorded over the previous 10 to 20 years.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers used instruments carried into the atmosphere by balloons launched from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected measurements with the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical instrument designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone directly above the South Pole fell to its lowest concentration of the year on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

articles.title: JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe
articles.dek: How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy.
paragraphs: How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy. Black holes weighing about a billion solar masses within the first billion years of the universe require extraordinary origin stories.

Now, a new multiwavelength study of a potential black hole may offer a clue. Combining spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) with Hubble imaging and archival data from the Very Large Telescope's MUSE instrument, astronomers identified this black hole in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy as seen about 12 billion years ago. This black hole appears to have a mass of about 3. 3 million suns and sits in a galaxy containing roughly 145 million solar masses in stars. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server, explains why this is unusual.

Many recent studies have revealed early black holes that have a different relationship with their host galaxies, compared to what's seen in the nearby universe. Early black holes are too heavy compared to their host galaxies' stellar masses. This suggests the black holes in the early universe may grow quicker than the stars.

Researchers point out another factor that may affect the 'overmassive black holes' sample. Surveys can only detect black holes that are bright or fast-moving enough, so the samples have the heaviest ones for a given galaxy mass. Those giant black holes are only the tip of the iceberg. To really understand how black holes form and grow, astronomers need to look for the smaller, more typical ones too. But these are also hard to detect.

The signals from supernovae exploding into dense gas, shocks, and outflows can mimic faint black holes. In young, metal-poor galaxies, the spectral line ratios used to differentiate black hole-powered gas from star-powered gas may overlap, and extreme stars can mimic an active galactic nucleus (AGN), a galaxy powered by a massive black hole.

In the new study, Mirko Curti of the INAF—Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna and colleagues used many lines of evidence rather than one to ask whether the object at the center of MARTA 3887 is an overmassive black hole.

Using the spectroscopic observations from JWST, they detected a wide hydrogen-alpha line, which revealed that the gas is moving at about 1,270 kilometers per second (790 miles per second). The signal appeared only in hydrogen, not in other kinds of lines such as those from oxygen that come from calmer gas. This pointed to a black hole rather than an ordinary outflow.

Next, they estimated the black hole's mass: roughly 3. 3 million times the sun's mass. This mass estimate places it among the lower-mass black holes found by JWST. The galaxy, on the other hand, has about 145 million solar masses of stars, so the black hole is roughly 2. 3% of the stellar mass.

Researchers note that this relation is "approximately 2 dex above the local relation," which means it is about 100 times higher than the relationship extrapolated from nearby galaxies. This suggests that "black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component," the team writes in the paper.

The galaxy itself is compact and clumpy and is low in heavy elements, about 10% of the sun's level, which is typical of a young galaxy. It is forming stars fast, roughly five to nine solar masses of new stars per year, mostly in a recent burst.

articles.title: Ancient Meteorites May Have Delivered One of Life’s Most Essential Ingredients to Earth
articles.dek: Ancient meteorites may hold the key to understanding when and how Earth acquired one of life’s most essential elements.
paragraphs: Ancient meteorites may hold the key to understanding when and how Earth acquired one of life’s most essential elements.

Carbon erupting from Hawaiian volcanoes may have originated deep within Earth’s metallic core, carrying a chemical fingerprint that dates back to the planet’s formation. A new study suggests that carbon-rich meteorites delivered a substantial amount of Earth’s carbon during its early history, potentially helping supply the element that would eventually become essential to life.

Researchers analyzing volcanic rocks from Hawaii identified an unusual carbon isotope signature that may trace back to Earth’s core. “We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth’s core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface,” says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor at Columbia University’s Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .

The researchers examined volcanic rocks from Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift, two Hawaiian volcanic systems that draw magma from different regions of the mantle. Samples from the Tantalus Rift contained carbon isotope signatures of approximately -5 to -7 per mil, consistent with typical mantle carbon. Kīlauea’s samples, however, had a much heavier signature of approximately -1 per mil, a value rarely observed in previous measurements.

“This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle,” says Moussallam. “This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.” Although the team considers the core the most likely source, the isotope measurements do not establish that origin conclusively.

Earth’s mantle extends roughly 1,800 miles beneath the crust, separating the surface from the planet’s metallic core. Scientists believe much of Earth’s carbon resides in the core, which cannot be directly sampled. However, research suggests that some materials from the liquid outer core may cross into the mantle and eventually reach the surface through mantle plumes. These rising columns of hot rock can partially melt as they approach the crust, supplying magma to volcanoes. Kīlauea is thought to receive magma from near the center of a plume that originates close to the core-mantle boundary, while the Tantalus Rift samples appear to represent the plume’s outer regions.

To investigate the carbon carried by these magmas, Moussallam’s team used a recently developed technique to measure carbon isotopes inside tiny pockets of trapped melt. As magma cools, growing crystals can enclose droplets of molten rock before dissolved gases escape. These sealed pockets, called undegassed melt inclusions, preserve carbon dioxide from the original magma. “These melts are fossils of the magma,” Moussallam says.

The researchers then compared Kīlauea’s unusual carbon signature with measurements from ancient meteorites. Moussallam argues that carbon preserved in Earth’s core should reflect “the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.” The closest similarities appeared in carbonaceous chondrites, a carbon-rich class of meteorites associated with the outer regions of the early solar system.

Chondrites contain some of the solar system’s oldest surviving material, dating back more than 4. 5 billion years. “All of Earth is made of chondrites,” Moussallam explains. “They’re the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.” Scientists distinguish between noncarbonaceous chondrites, associated with the inner solar system, and carbonaceous chondrites, which formed farther from the Sun. How much each group contributed to Earth’s formation remains debated.

The researchers propose that carbonaceous chondrites struck Earth relatively late in its formation, when the growing planet was better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have entered the core before eventually moving into the mantle and reaching the surface through volcanic activity. The isotope similarities support this possibility, but confirming that the carbon actually originated in the core will require additional evidence. “We don’t really know. We need more measurements,” cautions Moussallam.

The proposed journey would connect carbon delivered by ancient meteorites, stored deep inside Earth, and eventually released into the environment where living organisms could incorporate it. “It’s fun to think about. We’re made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet’s core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.”

articles.title: Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
articles.dek: A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.
paragraphs: A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers —one European, the other Japanese—will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1. 7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany—94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away—could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.
BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury—the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon—and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can't wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare "unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time," he noted.

Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's smaller craft will study Mercury's dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers).

The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year—or the equivalent of four Mercury years.
"The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself," Jones said in an email.
Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system's least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors—a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s.

articles.title: COP31 fails to agree on climate deal in chaotic finale
articles.dek: The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into…
paragraphs: The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into record overtime in Turkey.
The main deal was rejected by a host of nations 44 hours after the summit's official close in a chaotic COP31 finale in the Turkish city of Antalya.

"We will not endorse a cover decision ... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.
COP31 President Murat Kurum conceded the deal had failed to reach consensus.
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," he told the closing session.

Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks, which come against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war between the United States and Iran that has roiled the Middle East.
Language around fossil fuels is fiercely opposed by petrostates such as Saudi Arabia.
With expectations low, negotiations chief Australia had sought an overarching "cover decision" to capture what countries agreed at COP31 and send a signal about the future course of climate action.
But the final proposal failed to mention coal, oil and gas at all, plunging the summit into turmoil as it broke the record for the longest-ever U. N. climate conference.

"We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future," the Marshall Islands climate envoy Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner told delegates.
Panama, a vocal critic of the U. N. climate talks, Vanuatu and Belize also rejected the pact.
Outside the assembly hall, O'Brien told AFP the summit had been "hijacked by some oil states."
Decisions at the U. N. climate talks are taken by consensus, meaning just one of the nearly 200 nations involved can block agreement.
Threats of a walkout Saturday prompted Turkey and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the European Union and Saudi Arabia, but a compromise remained elusive.

articles.title: Hybrid nanocrystal surface reveals new way to tune interactions with infrared light
articles.dek: A one-crystal-thick sheet made from two types of nanocrystals mixed in solution can amplify or suppress infrared light beyond the sum of its parts.
paragraphs: A one-crystal-thick sheet made from two types of nanocrystals mixed in solution can amplify or suppress infrared light beyond the sum of its parts.

Known as a metasurface, this sheet contains randomly mixed nanocrystals—made of indium oxide doped with 1% or 3% tin—that interact with one another and infrared light to produce the superlinear optical effect.

Experimental results helped the team build a model that other researchers can use as a design tool, allowing them to choose the optimal doping levels and mixing ratios of nanoparticles to achieve certain light-matter interactions.

Specifically, incoming infrared light stirs up waves of electrons, called plasmons, on the metasurface that trap light on the nanocrystals and in the tiny gaps between them. Depending on the infrared light's frequency, the mismatched electron waves of neighboring 1% and 3% indium tin oxide (ITO) nanocrystals either boost or suppress that trapped energy.

"We used different techniques and different theoretical backgrounds, and even though we studied them independently at first, eventually everything pointed toward a single theory and a single phenomenon," said Yujin Park, a postdoctoral research fellow of chemical engineering at U-M and lead author of the study published in ACS Nano .

This collaborative study included researchers from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, University of Texas at Austin, University of Colorado Boulder and Institució Catalana de Recerca i Estudis Avançats (ICREA) in Barcelona, Spain.

The U-M team first observed the deviations from linear optical effects with a far-field infrared spectroscopy technique. An infrared light source shines on the material as a whole, effectively averaging out the interactions among all the tiny crystals.

The researchers brought the light source closer, known as a near-field technique, to understand how optical responses vary across the metasurface in small clusters of nanocrystals using synchrotron infrared nanospectroscopy, or SINS for short, at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. SINS revealed that absorption varied from spot to spot depending on each particle's immediate neighbors.

The electron beam in a powerful electron microscope at Oak Ridge National Laboratory zoomed in even closer with subnanometer precision. The technique mapped plasmon energy patterns around individual nanocrystals, confirming that the 1% and 3% ITO nanocrystals were truly randomly mixed and showing how neighboring particles interact to change how the material absorbs light.

The 3% ITO nanocrystals produce higher-energy plasmon waves compared to 1% ITO nanocrystals. Like tuning forks of two different pitches vibrating in water, their ripples overlap in the 2. 5-nanometer gaps between nanocrystals—reinforcing each other at some incoming infrared light frequencies and dampening each other at others.

"There are things that are invisible to light that become very obvious in the electron beam. We could readily differentiate the nanocrystals doped with 3% tin from the ones doped with 1% tin based on the way they interact with the electron beam, an interaction that's completely invisible with light," said Delia Milliron, the James and Judith Street Professor of Chemical Engineering at U-M and a senior author of the study.

"The experimental data from this study validate the physical picture predicted from electromagnetic simulations, paving the way for computation-guided engineering of nanocrystal-based plasmonic metasurfaces," said Thomas Truskett, the Vennema Professor of Chemical Engineering at U-M and a senior author of the study.
Importantly, manufacturing metasurfaces in solution sidesteps the limitations of expensive, top-down manufacturing like etching microscopic patterns on a surface, helping scale up the technology.

articles.title: SpaceX Dragon Returns to Earth With a Treasure Trove of Scientific Secrets
articles.dek: A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft has returned to Earth carrying an unusual collection of scientific cargo, including cancer research samples, 3D-printed blood vessels, and bacteria…
paragraphs: A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft has returned to Earth carrying an unusual collection of scientific cargo, including cancer research samples, 3D-printed blood vessels, and bacteria studied in space. The experiments could provide valuable insights into human health, lead to better medical treatments, and help astronauts stay healthy on future missions.
The uncrewed capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles at 2:03 p. m. PST, successfully completing NASA’s 35th SpaceX commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station.

Dragon departed the orbiting laboratory at 11:05 a. m. CST on November 20, bringing back research materials that scientists can now examine in detail on Earth. Unlike many spacecraft that deliver supplies to the station, Dragon is also designed to return cargo safely, making it especially valuable for experiments that require further laboratory analysis.
Among the returning experiments is a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct created to investigate how blood vessels age and how cardiovascular diseases develop.

Bioprinting is a technology that uses living cells and specialized materials to build structures resembling human tissue. By studying these blood vessel models in microgravity, where objects experience near weightlessness, researchers hope to gain a better understanding of biological changes that may affect people both in space and on Earth.

Dragon also carried frozen tumor organoids that had undergone experimental treatments aboard the space station. Organoids are small, laboratory-grown models that reproduce certain characteristics of human tissues or tumors, allowing scientists to investigate diseases and test potential therapies.

Researchers hope these samples will reveal information that could improve cancer treatments and support personalized medicine, an approach that aims to tailor medical care to the characteristics of individual patients.

Another set of experiments focuses on antibiotic resistance, a growing medical concern worldwide. Frozen microbial samples returned aboard Dragon will help scientists examine how bacteria that resist antibiotic treatments survive, adapt, and evolve in the unusual environment of space.

Understanding these changes could be important for protecting astronauts on extended missions, when access to medical care is limited. The findings may also offer useful insights into how antibiotic-resistant microbes behave.

The returning cargo included a specialized lighting system that spent more than three years aboard the space station. Researchers used the equipment to investigate how lighting could improve astronauts’ sleep and overall well-being during long missions.

Light plays an important role in regulating the body’s internal clock, which influences when people feel alert or sleepy. Maintaining a healthy sleep schedule can be especially challenging aboard the space station, which circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes and experiences numerous sunrises and sunsets each day.

The spacecraft’s journey began on October 13, when it launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Dragon reached the International Space Station two days later, on October 15.
After spending more than a month at the orbiting laboratory, the spacecraft returned with scientific samples and equipment ready for further examination.

Although the experiments have not yet established new medical breakthroughs, the research could contribute to advances in cancer treatment, cardiovascular health, infectious disease research, and astronaut safety. The results may ultimately benefit patients on Earth while helping NASA prepare for longer journeys deeper into space.

articles.title: Milky Way simulation reaches record resolution with the help of three supercomputers

A team of researchers, including those from the University of Tokyo, have developed a new way to model the Milky Way at a level of detail never achieved before. They simulated the entire galaxy down to the level of individual stars by combining the power of some of the world's most powerful supercomputers using an AI-accelerated model that works on a variety of hardware platforms. Their methods can improve our understanding of galactic evolution.
Their paper was presented at the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis ( SC 2026 ), held Nov. 15–20 in Chicago.

It's nice to know where we came from and where we're going. This is true in ways we can see on different timescales: day to day, year to year, century to century, or even longer periods too. On the galactic level, scales of time and space can be so vast they become difficult to model. Galaxies contain hundreds of billions of stars, as well as gas and other materials, all interacting under gravity and other forces.

That means simulations are always based on models that are simplified in some way, often in temporal resolution or spatial complexity, because the more closely you try to represent everything we see in the galaxy, especially at small timescales, the more computing power is required. This is particularly challenging in a galaxy as large as the Milky Way, where small regions can change rapidly and demand many more calculation steps than the rest of the galaxy.

"We expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way–sized galaxy, it's not straightforward," said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo.

"When we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required. We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves. This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

They call the simulation PHEASANT, and the key to the approach is an AI model developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. When a star goes supernova , it heats and pushes surrounding gas outward. Simulating this process in detail normally requires very small time steps. Hirashima's AI model predicts how the gas will change over time, allowing the main galaxy simulation to skip many of these smaller calculations.

According to the researchers, this makes the simulation around 20 times faster than directly calculating the same process in the usual exhaustive way. The team's most recent key development was to adapt their software to work efficiently on three different supercomputer systems, using different kinds of hardware including a mixture of CPUs and GPUs from different makers.

"One of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years," said Hirashima. "My model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation.

"Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations."

articles.title: A Common Meat Triggers a Unique Muscle-Building Peptide, Study Finds
articles.dek: A new study found that lean ground pork triggered a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle growth.
paragraphs: A new study found that lean ground pork triggered a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle growth.

A new study suggests that the way the body processes protein after exercise may depend on more than how much protein a meal contains. Researchers found that lean ground pork produced a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle protein synthesis, the biological process responsible for building and repairing muscle proteins.

Published in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research , the research examined how different protein sources affect amino acids and peptides circulating in the bloodstream after resistance exercise. The findings suggest that the structure and composition of whole foods may influence how protein is digested and made available to the body.
Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign analyzed blood samples and muscle protein synthesis measurements from two randomized controlled trials involving healthy young adults.

Following resistance exercise, participants consumed one of five nutritional treatments: low-fat ground pork, high-fat ground pork, black beans and rice, an isolated nutrient beverage containing amino acids and other nutrients, or a carbohydrate-only control drink. Each protein-containing treatment supplied approximately 20 grams (0. 7 ounces) of protein, allowing researchers to compare the body’s responses to different nutritional sources.

Among the five treatments, lean ground pork was the only one to produce a statistically significant increase above baseline in circulating dileucine, a peptide composed of two linked leucine molecules. Blood concentrations rose approximately 90 to 120 minutes after consumption. Dileucine has been associated with muscle protein synthesis, although scientists are still investigating its specific role in muscle metabolism.

Peak dileucine concentrations after lean ground pork consumption were significantly higher than those measured after the isolated nutrient beverage and carbohydrate control. However, the differences compared with high-fat ground pork and the beans-and-rice meal were not statistically significant.

Lean ground pork also produced the highest peak concentrations of leucine, an essential amino acid involved in regulating muscle protein synthesis. These levels were significantly higher than those following high-fat ground pork, beans and rice, or the carbohydrate control, but were not significantly different from the isolated nutrient beverage.

“These findings suggest that the body’s response to protein is influenced by more than the amount consumed,” said Nicholas A. Burd, PhD, corresponding author and researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Seeing how the whole-food matrix affects the release of amino acids and peptides into the bloodstream gives us a clearer picture of how dietary protein may actually drive muscle protein synthesis and remodeling.”

Across the protein-containing treatments, researchers identified a modest but statistically significant positive relationship between peak dileucine concentrations and changes in muscle protein synthesis. The same association was not observed with conventional leucine measurements.
Importantly, this does not establish that dileucine directly stimulates muscle growth or that lean ground pork produces greater muscle gains than other foods.

One possible explanation involves the food matrix, which encompasses a food’s physical structure and the interactions among its components. Researchers proposed that grinding meat could disrupt connective tissue, potentially making proteins more accessible to digestive enzymes and changing how amino acids and peptides enter the bloodstream.

The results add to research investigating how whole-food protein sources influence the body’s response to exercise. Although the protein content of a meal remains relevant, differences in food structure, fat content, and digestion may affect the timing and composition of nutrients reaching the bloodstream.

“Consumers often think about protein in terms of how many grams are on their plate, but science is showing us there is much more to the story,” said Kristen Hicks-Roof, PhD, RDN, LDN, Senior Director of Human Nutrition at the National Pork Board. “What’s exciting about this research is that it helps us better understand how a familiar food like ground pork delivers protein and how the body responds to it after exercise. Ground pork represents an important opportunity to connect emerging protein science with practical, nutritious meals people already enjoy.”

articles.title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
articles.dek: The U. S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice .
paragraphs: The U. S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice . According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide , an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “ unacceptable risk of accidental detonation .” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed after the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026 . A federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued, but the U. S. Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.
The Justice Department told the court in a response late on Nov. 21 that the Army intends to carry out the detonations by Nov. 24, 2026 . A precise date and time weren’t immediately released.

To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets .

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children . If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies , including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth , where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body . That’s a pretty strong statement.
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23 , the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
articles.dek: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.
paragraphs: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U. S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U. S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1. 3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.
Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc. , selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
articles.dek: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.
paragraphs: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U. S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U. S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1. 3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.
Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc. , selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.
